places.nameTh: วัดแม่พระลูกประคำ (กาลหว่าร์)
places.photoAlt: Trilingual Holy Rosary Church entrance sign across a driveway.
places.source: Talat Noi research brief, review of 11 Nov 2026. Sources are listed on the card.
places.storyEn:
After Ayutthaya fell in 1767, Portuguese Catholics travelled down the Chao Phraya to the Bangkok area. A group settled on the east bank, on land later granted for their church in the reign of Rama I. They brought two devotional figures from Ayutthaya: Our Lady of the Rosary and a figure of Christ after the crucifixion. The older name, Kalawar, comes from Calvary, the place associated with the crucifixion.

The first church was completed in 1787, after the land grant the previous year. Its successor was consecrated in 1839 and formally dedicated to Our Lady of the Rosary. By then, Chinese Catholics, including Teochew residents, were becoming an important part of parish life. That change is one reason the Thai, Chinese and English lettering at the gate feels at home here.

The present church is the third building, completed in 1897. Its pointed arches, tall cross-topped spire and stained glass belong to the Gothic Revival style. Notice that the main front faces the river, a reminder of how much of the old city was approached by water.

โบสถ์ที่เห็นในปัจจุบันเป็นหลังที่สาม สร้างเสร็จใน พ.ศ. 2440 ลองสังเกตยอดแหลม ซุ้มโค้ง และกระจกสีแบบกอทิกฟื้นฟู ด้านหน้าของโบสถ์หันสู่แม่น้ำ เหมือนชวนให้นึกถึงสมัยที่ผู้คนเดินทางมาทางน้ำ

places.location: Around Soi Wanit 2 and Charoen Krung Soi 22, Talat Noi, Samphanthawong
places.nameTh: ย่านการค้าเก่าตลาดน้อย
places.source: Talat Noi research brief, review of 11 Nov 2026. Sources are listed on the card.
places.storyEn:
In early Bangkok, trade spread south from the busy Sampeng market. The smaller market that grew here became known locally as Ta Lak Kia, or Talat Noi: “little market.” The river linked the quarter to the movement of people and goods. Chinese merchants, laborers and artisans put down roots here, with Hokkien, Hakka and Teochew communities among them. The nearby Catholic church and Chinese shrines show how different communities made their lives along the same river.

Commerce here went beyond selling goods. River traffic gave metalworkers a reason to make and repair fittings for boats. The neighborhood later became associated with Xiang Kong, the trade in used machinery and vehicle parts. Look at the small spaces between a home, a storefront and a workshop: each tells you how work and daily life share the same streets.

For a deeper introduction, the Treasury Department’s Talat Noi Museum occupies the site of a former lathe workshop. The museum building was designed to recall that workshop. Its neighborhood exhibits give the lanes you have just walked through a little more meaning.

places.location: 282 Soi Duang Tawan, off Soi Wanit 2, Talat Noi
places.nameTh: คฤหาสน์โซวเฮงไถ่
places.photoAlt: Entrance of So Heng Tai Mansion, photographed in 2020
places.source: Talat Noi research brief, review of 11 Nov 2026. Sources are listed on the card.
places.storyEn:
The story of this house is tied to Chao Sua Jat, a Hokkien merchant known by the title Phra Aphai Wanit. Creative Thailand records his involvement in collecting government revenue on edible bird’s nests and links his family to river commerce. Generations of the Posayachinda family have looked after the compound. Think of it as a home shaped by the fortunes and choices of a family over time.

The arrangement helps explain how the household worked: the gateway opens into a central yard with rooms around it. The three wings make a U around the courtyard, with the entrance structure closing the fourth side. The house is often described as *si ruean lom lan*, or “four structures around a courtyard.” Architectural research describes Hokkien planning combined with Siamese building elements.

The pool in the courtyard is a later addition made for diving. It is one of the ways the family adapted the old compound to new uses. Researchers who interviewed the family describe the work and cost of looking after a private heritage house. The house still has a life of its own beyond the hours visitors may be able to enter.

places.location: Trok San Chao Rong Kueak, off Soi Wanit 2, beside the Chao Phraya
places.nameTh: ศาลเจ้าโรงเกือก (ฮ้อนหว่องกุง)
places.photoAlt: Rong Kueak Shrine front exterior and forecourt, photographed in 2021
places.source: Talat Noi research brief, review of 11 Nov 2026. Sources are listed on the card.
places.storyEn:
Rong Kueak is a Hakka shrine dedicated to Hon Wong Kung. Stone plaques inside record an older tradition: Hakka merchants brought the image of the deity from China before the present shrine existed. The tourism department’s account describes worshippers outgrowing the original shrine for processions. In the late nineteenth century, the committee raised money to purchase riverside land next to it, making room for the community to gather.

Take a closer look at the entrance. Small framed panels combine narrative painting with tile-decorated stucco. Carved wooden panels beside the doorway include dragon and cloud motifs; the tourism directory describes them as part of the shrine’s “dragon and tiger window” design. Inside, the museum also records the presence of Pun Thao Kong, a deity associated with prosperity.

The shrine has a different community history from Chow Sue Kong, the Hokkien shrine elsewhere in Talat Noi. Seeing both gives the walk a richer sense of the Chinese communities that settled here.

places.location: Public lanes around Trok San Chao Rong Kueak and Soi Duang Tawan, near Soi Wanit 2
places.nameTh: ตรอกสตรีทอาร์ตและงานช่างตลาดน้อย
places.source: Talat Noi research brief, review of 11 Nov 2026. Sources are listed on the card.
places.storyEn:
Start with the work behind the walls. On a river that carried goods and boats, local smiths made and repaired parts such as anchors and chains. In its portrait project, the Creative Economy Agency profiled a Talat Noi smith who learned the work from his father and later took on smaller jobs such as tools for craftspeople. The used-parts trade adds another chapter: one part that is surplus to one repair can be useful to the next.

The walls carry stories of their own. In a 2022 interview, a neighborhood tourism organizer recalled gaining permission to paint on a long Marine Department wall. One of the images recalled the red-prowed trading junks once associated with the river. A 2018 community art project included a golden lion by Bonus TMC and a turtle by DR.CAS, drawing on lion dancing, shrine celebrations and ritual food. The street has also displayed photography from the 2020 Bangkok Design Week period. These are documented examples from different years; what you see on any given walk can change.

places.location: 758 Soi Phanu Rangsi (ภาณุรังษี), Talat Noi
places.nameTh: ศาลเจ้าโจวซือกง
places.photoAlt: Facade of Chow Sue Kong Shrine, photographed in 2021
places.source: Talat Noi research brief, review of 11 Nov 2026. Sources are listed on the card.
places.storyEn:
An inscription dates the shrine to 1804, in the reign of Rama I. For the Hokkien community, it was a place to gather and keep religious traditions after settling in Bangkok. Chow Sue Kong is the local name associated with Qingshui Zushi (清水祖師), revered in Fujian and often called the “Divine Doctor” here. Worshippers traditionally come with hopes for health, well-being and good fortune.

Look at the shrine’s orientation toward the Chao Phraya and the detailed stucco, which TAT describes as retaining Qing-style features. The shrine is closely associated with Talat Noi’s Vegetarian Festival. During Yuanxiao, after Lunar New Year, worshippers also bring *khanom tao*. A study of the ritual describes Talat Noi’s version as a white, bun-like wheat pastry in the shape of a turtle, a symbol of long life. It is a small detail that connects the shrine, household cooking and the stories painted in nearby lanes.
places.storyTh:

places.nameTh: มุมจัดแสดงหุ่นยนต์หน้าเวิร์กช็อป
places.photoAlt: Red-and-gold and dark metal robot sculptures beside an orange shopfront with red lanterns.
places.source: Talat Noi research brief, review of 11 Nov 2026. Sources are listed on the card.
places.storyEn:
The first thing you might notice is the red-and-gold figure. Then your eye moves to the dark metal figures beside it: pointed shoulders, layered plates and feet built up in pieces. The orange shopfront and lanterns make the display feel like part of the lane. The photo also shows stacks of parts behind the sculptures.

There is a local story behind that juxtaposition. Talat Noi became known for dealing in used machinery and vehicle parts, a trade called Xiang Kong. In a published interview, parts trader Aree Manatpakorn, known as Hia Seng Junior, described making other robot sculptures from reclaimed components. The trade helps explain why metal and machines appear so often in the neighborhood’s newer art. The maker of the specific figures in this field photo still needs to be confirmed.
places.storyTh: ในภาพมีทั้งหุ่นสีแดงทอง หุ่นโลหะสีเข้ม และกองชิ้นส่วนอยู่ด้านหลัง ภาพนี้ชวนให้นึกถึงเซียงกง การค้าเครื่องจักรและอะไหล่มือสองที่ผูกกับตลาดน้อยมานาน ในย่านเดียวกันมีตัวอย่างงานหุ่นที่นำอะไหล่เก่ามาทำใหม่ แต่ผู้สร้างหุ่นในภาพนี้ยังต้องยืนยัน

A glass-fronted cart sits under an awning, with trays and neatly stacked ingredients visible inside. Next to it are metal tables with condiments, backed by pale green tiles. In a lane this narrow, a kitchen counter, a dining spot and a route home can be only a few steps apart.

A table beside a doorway and a cart pulled up under cover tell their own story about daily life here. This is a glimpse from Jump’s walk; the vendor’s name and menu are still being checked.

places.nameTh: กะหรี่ปั๊บคุณปุ๊
places.photoAlt: Teal folding doorway and tables of packaged snacks at Khun Pu’s Curry Puffs.
places.source: Talat Noi research brief, review of 11 Nov 2026. Sources are listed on the card.
places.storyEn:
Khun Pu is Ratchanee Sae Tia. She learned to make curry puffs at a vocational training center, then tested and adapted the recipe until it was her own. In an interview she recalled getting feedback from people who tried the pastries. She started with a chicken filling and went on to make other fillings. A small red dot pattern was used to help tell them apart.

The shop’s story also has a newer chapter. In the Creative Economy Agency’s *Made in Charoenkrung* project, Khun Pu worked with Nosh.nosh Project and illustrator Jirayu Koo on new fillings and takeaway packaging. It is an example of an everyday neighborhood snack growing through both practice and collaboration.

places.nameTh: โสรยา ลาบ 101
places.photoAlt: Green-fronted Soraya Larb 101 stall, with a Thai menu sign and stacked colorful stools.
places.source: Talat Noi research brief, review of 11 Nov 2026. Sources are listed on the card.
places.storyEn:
The sign on the stall reads โสรยา ลาบ 101. It names several familiar Isan dishes: *som tam*, a pounded papaya salad; *larb*, a chopped meat salad seasoned with herbs; and *kai yang*, grilled chicken. It also lists *nam tok* and sticky rice. The mortar printed on the sign and the woven rice containers in the photo give you a few clues to the meal before you order.

This stop shows another strand of everyday Bangkok food. The combination of green papaya salad, grilled chicken and sticky rice is associated with Isan and neighboring Laos. It works well as a shared meal: one dish bright and sharp, another grilled, with sticky rice alongside.

places.nameTh: หุ่นบัมเบิลบีหน้าโบสถ์กาลหว่าร์
places.photoAlt: Yellow Bumblebee sculpture on a low paved island with the Holy Rosary Church gateway behind it.
places.source: Talat Noi research brief, review of 11 Nov 2026. Sources are listed on the card.
places.storyEn:
This yellow figure is Bumblebee, one of the robot sculptures made by local used-parts trader Aree Manatpakorn, known as Hia Seng Junior. In a 2025 interview, he explained that the idea came out of a conversation about making a neighborhood landmark that would recall the Xiang Kong trade. The reclaimed parts differ from piece to piece, so the shapes come from what the makers have to work with.

Heritage researcher Alisa Santikarn documented Bumblebee in front of Holy Rosary Church after the figure moved from a different roundabout where Optimus Prime took its place. Jump's photo shows the yellow figure on the paved island with the church sign behind it. The juxtaposition is worth a look: an old faith community and a new piece of neighborhood craft in the same frame.
places.storyTh: บัมเบิลบีเป็นหนึ่งในหุ่นที่อารี มนัสภากร หรือเฮียเซ้ง จูเนียร์ ทำขึ้นจากแนวคิดนำอะไหล่เก่ามาสร้างจุดจดจำของย่านเซียงกง นักวิจัยด้านมรดกบันทึกว่าหุ่นเคยอยู่ที่วงเวียนอีกจุดหนึ่ง ก่อนย้ายมาบริเวณหน้าโบสถ์กาลหว่าร์

places.photoAlt: Three mounted photographs on a weathered lane wall, including a print of Haroon Mosque.
places.source: Talat Noi research brief, review of 11 Nov 2026. Sources are listed on the card.
places.storyEn:
In Jump’s photo, prints hang from simple metal brackets against a worn wall. One picture shows the entrance of Haroon Mosque. Its printed caption identifies the *Portrait of Charoenkrung* project. Another shows a person in red looking out from a railing. Take a moment to look at how each photograph makes a different part of the area feel close.

The Creative Economy Agency records *Portrait of Charoenkrung* as a 2020 project about the district’s residents, families, work and traditions. The photography reached into public space during Bangkok Design Week. The tourism directory documents the exhibition in the shrine lane, and reporting from the event describes photographs installed along its wall. The project gives the walk something you cannot get from architecture alone: a look at the people who give the neighborhood its character.
places.storyTh: โครงการ Portrait of Charoenkrung บันทึกครอบครัว อาชีพ และวิถีชีวิตในย่านเจริญกรุงเมื่อ พ.ศ. 2563 ภาพบางส่วนเคยจัดแสดงในตรอกช่วง Bangkok Design Week ในภาพภาคสนามของ Jump มีภาพทางเข้ามัสยิดฮารูณอยู่บนกำแพงด้วย เป็นเรื่องของสถานที่ในภาพ ไม่ใช่ตำแหน่งของกำแพง

places.photoAlt: Wooden doors with Mother Roaster and Elephant Parade signs beneath a yellow mural marked 1172.
places.source: Talat Noi research brief, review of 11 Nov 2026. Sources are listed on the card.
places.storyEn:
Mother Roaster began with Ploenpit Rianmek, better known as Pa Pim. In an interview she described taking up coffee seriously after retirement, experimenting with roasting, grinding and brewing by hand at a small coffee stand. Her story is an easy one to connect with: a daily pleasure became something she wanted to learn more about and share.

By 2020, the Talat Noi café was documented in the upper floor of a wooden building associated with spare parts. Visitors passed metal components on the way upstairs. The building made room for a new use while keeping clues to the work that had been done there. Look for the weathered double doors and the yellow mural in the photo. In the fieldwork photo, the Mother Roaster sign hangs beside an Elephant Parade sign.

places.location: Soi Duang Tawan, near So Heng Tai Mansion
places.nameTh: ภาพผนังวิถีตลาดน้อย
places.photoAlt: Painted rickshaw passenger eating noodles and a blacksmith with a hammer, behind parked scooters.
places.source: Talat Noi research brief, review of 11 Nov 2026. Sources are listed on the card.
places.storyEn:
Follow the painted scene from left to right. A passenger in red eats from a bowl while a rickshaw puller leans into his work. Nearby, a blacksmith raises a hammer at a glowing hearth. The characters make the wall playful, but the details also invite you to notice the work that keeps a street going.

The blacksmith scene has a documented connection to the neighborhood, even though the artist’s intention for this wall has not been confirmed. The Creative Economy Agency records Talat Noi smiths making anchors, chains and other fittings for boats that came in by river. The painted forge is a good cue to think about that history as you pass today’s shopfronts.
places.storyTh: ในภาพมีคนนั่งกินก๋วยเตี๋ยวบนรถลาก คนลากรถที่เอนตัวไปข้างหน้า และช่างที่ยกค้อนอยู่หน้าเตา ภาพช่างชวนให้นึกถึงงานตีสมอ โซ่ และชิ้นส่วนเรือที่เคยมีบทบาทในตลาดน้อย
places.tipEn: Try spotting the noodle bowl and the hammer first. If scooters or cars are parked in front, enjoy what you can see without stepping into the traffic path.
places.tipTh: ลองหาชามก๋วยเตี๋ยวกับค้อนให้เจอก่อน หากมีรถจอดบังบางส่วน ให้ชมจากจุดที่ยืนได้โดยไม่กีดขวางทาง

places.nameTh: 32 บาร์ เอ็กซ์ สเปเชียลตี้ช็อกโกแลต
places.photoAlt: Wood-panelled shopfront of 32Bar X with a gold logo, a festive garland and tall glass doors looking into the glowing chocolate shop.
places.photoCaption: 32Bar X: award-winning chocolate, made right here in Talat Noi
places.source: Map team site visit: photo, coordinates and opening hours. Award and product details from the map team, not yet independently confirmed.
places.storyEn: Push open the tall wooden doors of 32Bar X and step into a chocolate lover's fantasy. This award-winning chocolatier makes its chocolate right here in Talat Noi, and every bite has a taste you won't find anywhere else: rich, surprising flavours you'll be thinking about long after you leave. The shop is a destination in itself. Warm wood, glowing counters piled high with treats and a jewel-bright chandelier give it the magical, anything-can-happen feel of a Willy Wonka sweet shop, right down to its very own chocolate vending machine. Best of all is the welcome: the team behind the counter is warm, friendly and full of personality, and happy to help you find your new favourite bar.
places.storyTh: ผลักประตูไม้บานสูงของ 32 บาร์ เอ็กซ์ แล้วก้าวเข้าสู่โลกในฝันของคนรักช็อกโกแลต ร้านช็อกโกแลตที่คว้ารางวัลมาแล้วแห่งนี้ผลิตช็อกโกแลตเองที่ตลาดน้อย ทุกคำมีรสชาติเฉพาะตัวที่หาไม่ได้จากที่อื่น เข้มข้น น่าประหลาดใจ และชวนให้คิดถึงไปอีกนาน ตัวร้านเองก็เป็นจุดหมายที่ต้องมาเยือน ทั้งงานไม้โทนอบอุ่น ตู้โชว์เปล่งแสงที่มีขนมหวานเรียงราย และโคมระย้าสีสดใส ให้บรรยากาศมหัศจรรย์ราวกับหลุดเข้าไปในร้านขนมของวิลลี่ วองก้า แถมยังมีตู้กดช็อกโกแลตอัตโนมัติให้ได้ลองอีกด้วย ที่ประทับใจที่สุดคือการต้อนรับ พนักงานอัธยาศัยดี เป็นกันเอง มีเสน่ห์ และยินดีช่วยคุณค้นหาช็อกโกแลตชิ้นโปรดชิ้นใหม่
places.tipEn: Open daily, 9:30 AM to 7:00 PM. Try the chocolate vending machine, ask the team which flavour they love most, and take a bar home: it makes the perfect Talat Noi souvenir.
